claims.claim: Your video can cross an ocean in a few dozen milliseconds, and nobody plans its whole route. No wire is reserved for it. No master map guides it. So what really carries it from your phone to your friend's screen?

No reserved circuit and per-datagram independence are confirmed by RFC 791. claims.claim: But IP promises nothing. Packets can arrive late, out of order, duplicated, or not at all. So a second protocol, TCP, sits on top to fix that. Cerf and Kahn designed TCP/IP so separately run networks could interconnect.

RFC 793 says TCP must recover from data that is damaged, lost, duplicated or delivered out of order. ISOC says Kahn, joined by Cerf in 1973, designed the protocol for open-architecture networking.

claims.claim: No office plans the whole route, and by design none keeps a record of each postcard's flow once it's passed on. This works because the internet is a huge number of separately run networks, like ISPs and universities, that interconnect and carry each other's traffic.
claims.correction: No office plans the whole route, and in the original design none keeps a record of each postcard's flow once it's passed on. This works because the internet is a huge number of separately run networks, like ISPs and universities, that interconnect and pass each other's traffic along.
claims.note: The Internet Society history says the original design kept gateways free of per-flow information, and that there is no global control at the operations level. 'By design' is too absolute for today's routers: they keep routing tables, and some routers record flow statistics. 'Carry each other's traffic' is a reasonable gloss on interconnection, but the sources say the networks connect and stand on their own. They do not literally say the networks agree to carry each other's traffic.

Traffic-engineering and congestion-aware routing do exist in some networks.

claims.note: Sequence numbers and retransmission are TCP features, not IP features. TCP numbers each octet, not each packet. A 'number on each piece' is an acceptable simplification for a general audience, though it does not name the layer. 'No dedicated line' is supported by RFC 791 ('no connections or logical circuits'). 'No master map' is a loose paraphrase: routers do hold routing tables, and the sources only say there is no global or centralized control. 'No central control' is what the sources state.

claims.claim: No dedicated line, no single master map, just one hop at a time, and a number on every piece so lost ones get resent. That design can help the internet keep working when parts of it break.
claims.correction: No dedicated line, no central control, just one hop at a time, and TCP numbers the data so lost pieces get resent. That design can help the internet keep working when parts of it break.
claims.note: 'No single master map' is a loose paraphrase. The sources support 'no centralized or global control' and 'no per-flow state kept in gateways', not the absence of any map. The resilience claim is hedged with 'can help', which is acceptable. The Internet Society page states the design goal that gateways keep no flow information, 'thereby keeping them simple and avoiding complicated adaptation and recovery from various failure modes.' RFC 1958 says the loss of state must not cause more than a temporary denial of service. 'A number on every piece' is TCP behavior (per octet), not a property of every packet on the internet. UDP traffic, for example, carries no such numbers.
